finding: §6.3 makes a specific, contradiction-prone claim — the emitted harness_note is the VERBATIM stored note, untrimmed; trimming applies only to the staleness comparisons. But the acceptance test that covers harness_note emission (Test 11, modified this round) pins only presence/absence ('emitted only when harness_stale is true ... never "" or null') and never asserts the emitted VALUE equals the untrimmed input. Two engineers write contradictory tests: given a stored note with leading/trailing whitespace that sets harness_stale, one asserts the emitted harness_note still carries that surrounding whitespace (per §6.3), the other asserts a trimmed value — both pass Test 11 as written.
suggestion: Add to Test 11 (or Test 10) an explicit assertion that the emitted harness_note is byte-for-byte the stored note including surrounding whitespace, while the trim applies only to the harness_stale non-empty/difference checks — e.g. record a note like ' framing A ' vs ' framing B ', assert harness_stale true and the emitted harness_note retains the leading/trailing spaces.

finding: The new over-specification class (§5) collides with §8.2 branch 3's mechanize_candidates advice. mechanize_candidates is the existing signal for a finding class that recurs (≥2 rounds, or ≥5 times in one round) and branch 3 emits the directive 'register a check (tp set --workflow checks=[…])'. But §5.2 defines over-specification as a non-mechanizable altitude smell whose correct resolution is moving detail into task acceptance, not authoring an automated shell check. If an over-specification finding recurs across rounds it satisfies the mechanize_candidates threshold and next_action would advise 'register a check', which is nonsensical for that class. The spec never excludes non-mechanizable classes (over-specification, and any pure-judgment class) from the mechanize_candidates array feeding branch 3, so an implementer building branch 3 from the array as-is would emit wrong advice.
suggestion: State whether over-specification (and other non-mechanizable classes) are excluded from the mechanize_candidates array that branch 3 reads, or clarify that branch 3's 'register a check' directive is scoped to classes representing mechanizable patterns and specify how tp distinguishes them.

finding: This round makes `over-specification` a canonical, reviewer-raised finding class (§5.2), and §5.1's whole failure mode is the spec *repeatedly* accreting mechanism — so `over-specification` is exactly the class most likely to recur and clear `mechanize_candidates`' purely frequency-based threshold (§8.2 branch 3: a class in >=2 rounds or >=5 times in one). When it does, `next_action` branch 3 spends the agent a directive: `register a check (tp set --workflow checks='[...]')`. But `over-specification` is by definition un-mechanizable — §5.2 defines it as 'a detail whose correctness can only be established against code' that belongs in task acceptance, and §10.3 states plainly that 'tp does not detect over-specification.' So the loop would advise authoring a spec-lint `cmd` for the one class no `cmd` can verify, contradicting §10.3 and burning a round-trip on an un-earned step that feeds no real decision. next_action's entire justification is naming a step the agent actually takes; here it names a dead end.
suggestion: Exclude the canonical `over-specification` class (and any class documented as reviewer-judgement-only) from `mechanize_candidates`, or add a clause to §8.2 branch 3 stating that a recurring `over-specification` class does not trigger the register-a-check directive (it falls through to branch 4, run the next round), so next_action never advises mechanizing a class §10.3 says tp does not detect.

finding: §5 (modified this round) introduces `over-specification` as a canonical finding `class` defined as 'a detail whose correctness can only be established against code, prescribed in the spec where it belongs in task acceptance instead' — i.e. altitude prose whose remedy is to push detail DOWN into task acceptance, explicitly NOT mechanizable by a spec-level check. But `over-specification` is a finding `class`, it is eligible for the `mechanize_candidates` array (§8.2 branch 3 / §11 test 14: a class recurring in ≥2 rounds or ≥5 times in one), and §5.1 states this class recurs by design ('across rounds the spec accretes implementation mechanism'). At low/medium severity it does not block (§5.2), so branch 3's precondition ('a `mechanize_candidates` class present, none blocking') is exactly met. `next_action` would then advise `register a check (tp set --workflow checks='[…]')` for a class whose whole thesis (§3 Principle 3, §5) is that no gate check can verify it and the correct response is to relocate the detail to acceptance — the opposite remedy. Test 14 would even pin this contradictory advice into a passing test when the recurring class is `over-specification`.
suggestion: Reconcile §8.2 branch 3 with §5: either exclude the canonical `over-specification` class from `mechanize_candidates` (it is definitionally unmechanizable), or state in §8.2/§5 that when the recurring class is `over-specification` the directive is 'push the detail into task acceptance and re-review' rather than 'register a check', so `next_action` never advises mechanizing an altitude finding.

finding: §8.2 branch 3 fires 'a mechanize_candidates class present, none blocking -> register a check', where mechanize_candidates is ANY finding class recurring in >=2 rounds (or >=5 times in one). The new over-specification class (§5) is precisely a class reviewers raise repeatedly across rounds, yet §10.3 states over-specification is NOT machine-detectable and is a reviewer judgement — so 'register a check (tp set --workflow checks=...)' is a nonsensical directive for it (no cmd can verify an altitude smell). The spec never excludes non-mechanizable classes from the mechanize_candidates set, so a test cannot decide whether next_action should emit branch 3 for a recurring over-specification class: two engineers write opposite assertions (branch 3 fires vs branch 4 fires).
suggestion: State explicitly whether over-specification (and any inherently non-mechanizable class) participates in mechanize_candidates / triggers branch 3, or is excluded so branch 4 governs; add a Test 14 case pinning next_action's output when over-specification is the only recurring class and none blocking.

finding: The set of commands that read/resolve review_converge_on is contradictory. §3.3 states 'The consuming commands are the ones that read the field — tp review --status/--record', but §9.4 requires the plain prompt-generation path (tp review <spec>, which emits role prompts) to render the enforced rule for the *resolved* review_converge_on ('under blocking they describe … no surviving critical or high … under all …'). Rendering the resolved value means the prompt-generation path must also resolve (and read) review_converge_on, making it a third consumer §3.3 never lists. Consequently the error behavior §3.3 specifies for consumers (an invalid *winning* value from a stored layer → validation error exit 1) is left unspecified for the prompt-generation path: an implementer cannot tell whether `tp review <spec>` with an invalid stored review_converge_on must abort exit 1 like --status/--record, or silently pick a fallback string.
suggestion: Reconcile the consumer enumeration: either add the prompt-generation path (tp review <spec>) to §3.3's list of commands that read review_converge_on and state its error behavior for an invalid winning value (presumably the same exit-1 validation), or, if the prompt string is meant to be static, drop §9.4's 'for the *resolved* review_converge_on' wording and describe both branches unconditionally.

finding: The round-15 fix widened §9.4 so the tool's convergence/instruction prompt strings now resolve to the active setting ('for the *resolved* review_converge_on ... under blocking ... under all ... for the active setting'), and Test 16 was updated to match ('match the resolved review_converge_on'). Because these convergence/instruction strings are emitted in the generated reviewer prompt (the plain `tp review <spec>` / `--perspective` prompt-generation path, not --status/--record), rendering them per the resolved value forces prompt generation to read review_converge_on. But unchanged §3.3 states categorically: 'The consuming commands are the ones that read the field - tp review --status/--record', and unchanged Test 17 lists only --status/--record as the commands that reject an invalid winning value (exit 1). In the round-15 baseline the prompt string was a fixed blocking-worded constant that did NOT read the field, so §3.3's enumeration was correct; the setting-aware rewrite introduces a new reader the enumeration excludes, and leaves the prompt-generation path's behavior on an invalid stored winning value unspecified.
suggestion: Reconcile the two sections. Either (a) add the prompt-generation path (plain `tp review <spec>` / `--perspective`) to §3.3's list of commands that read/resolve review_converge_on and specify its behavior on an invalid winning value (exit 1 like the other consumers, or a defined fallback to the blocking description), updating Test 17 accordingly; or (b) keep §9.4's prompt strings independent of the resolved value (e.g. always describe both policies, or the blocking default) so prompt generation need not read the field, keeping §3.3's reader set accurate.
